subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.textbook_anchor: My Favourite Food — Draw pictures of your favourite homemade food dishes and name them (p. 100)

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites children to close their eyes and think of a favourite homemade dish — what it looks like, smells like, tastes like. A few children share aloud before anyone draws, warming up the vocabulary of taste: sweet, sour, spicy, bitter.

Each child opens Textbook p. 100 and draws at least two favourite homemade food dishes, labelling each with its name. Children who finish quickly are invited to add colour or details that show why the dish is special.

Children share their drawings in pairs, explaining what taste each dish belongs to. The teacher walks the room, noting the variety of dishes that appear, and briefly introduces the idea that Indian festive traditions — like offering many foods together — celebrate this very variety of tastes.
A few pairs share with the whole class. The teacher collects one or two observations on the board: the different taste words used and the different occasions the food is made for.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent personal food knowledge through labelled drawings and connect dishes to taste categories.
periods.section_context: Favourite homemade food dishes, taste categories (sweet, sour, spicy, bitter), Chhappan Bhog tradition of 56 food items representing six tastes.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does anyone know of a time when many different foods are made together at once — maybe at a festival or celebration?' This draws out the Chhappan Bhog tradition naturally. Group children so that different home backgrounds sit together, maximising the diversity of dishes that surface.

periods.activity_title: Shirin's Diet — Balancing What We Eat
periods.textbook_anchor: Story of Shirin — the Runner — Discuss why we need to eat healthy food (p. 103)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of Shirin and her food items (p. 103)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the story of Shirin aloud (Textbook p. 103), pausing to ask children: 'What do you think is making Shirin fall sick so often?' Children predict before the story reveals its answer.

Children tick the food items in Textbook p. 103 that they eat regularly. In small groups they compare their ticks and identify which items nobody in their group eats — opening a discussion on food variety and what a balanced diet means.

The class discusses: 'Why do we need to eat healthy food?' Children name vegetables, fruits, grains — rice, ragi, jowar, wheat, bajra — pulses, and nuts, connecting these to Shirin's improved health. The teacher lists them on the board in categories the children suggest.

Children write two sentences in their notebooks: one food they eat regularly that keeps them strong, and one food they could add to eat a greater variety. The teacher closes by asking what Shirin ate before and what changed — reinforcing the link between variety and well-being without prescribing a diet.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain why variety across food groups supports physical well-being, using evidence from a narrative.
periods.section_context: Shirin the runner, balanced diet, food groups (vegetables, fruits, grains — rice, ragi, jowar, wheat, bajra — pulses, nuts), home-cooked varied diet, health and athletic performance.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you were Shirin's friend, what one food would you add to her lunch and why?' This keeps the discussion grounded in reasoning rather than recall. Ensure quieter children get a turn by using a paired share before whole-class sharing.

periods.activity_title: Seasonal and Regional Foods — Making a List
periods.textbook_anchor: We Eat Different Things — Make a list of fruits and vegetables available and special food items prepared in the summer and in the winter (p. 104)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 104 illustrations of seasonal produce

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks children to recall what they ate during the last summer holidays and what they eat now. A quick show of hands reveals that food changes with the season — cool drinks and juicy fruits appear in summer answers, warm soups and stews in winter answers.

Children open Textbook p. 104 and draw a two-column table in their notebooks: Summer and Winter. They list fruits, vegetables, and special food items prepared in each season, drawing on the textbook examples and their own home experience.

Pairs share their lists. The teacher guides a whole-class discussion on why certain produce appears only in certain seasons, and invites children to think about whether people in a different part of India might have a different summer list — building the near-to-far connection.

Children add one food item from another region of India to their winter or summer column — something they have tasted while travelling or heard about from a relative — and share it with the class. The teacher notes the regional variety on the board.

periods.implied_lo: Students can record and organise observations about how seasonal availability shapes food choices in their local and wider environment.
periods.section_context: Summer foods (cool drinks, juicy fruits, kulfi, tender coconut), winter foods (warm soups, stews), seasonal availability of produce, regional variation in food across India.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does anyone in your family say a food is only for a certain time of year — maybe because a grandparent insists on it?' This surfaces traditional seasonal food knowledge naturally. If children come from very different home regions, pair them deliberately to maximise the variety of regional examples.

periods.activity_title: Sorting Food by Its Source — Plant Parts
periods.textbook_anchor: Where does food come from? — Discuss and write down in what form some of these foods are cooked (p. 105)
materials: a small set of actual or pictured food items (carrot, spinach, mango, potato, rice, onion — or picture cards of these)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 105 diagram of plant parts with food examples

time_bands.activity: The teacher places the food items (or picture cards) on the desk and asks: 'What do all of these have in common?' After free responses, the question narrows: 'Which part of a plant does each one come from?' Children predict in pairs before looking at any reference.

Children open Textbook p. 105 and check their predictions against the plant-parts diagram. They draw a five-row table in their notebooks (roots, leaves, stems, seeds, fruits) and sort each food item into the correct row, writing both the item and the cooked form it commonly takes — e.g. carrot as raw salad or cooked sabzi.

Groups compare their tables. The teacher draws attention to items that surprised people — ginger as a stem, potato as a stem, bamboo shoots as a stem — and invites children to think of one more plant-part food they eat at home not already on the list.

Children write one puzzle question for a partner: 'I am a root / I am a seed — what am I?' Partners answer orally. The teacher closes by asking whether any item on their table could belong to two categories, sharpening classification thinking.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify everyday food items by the plant part they come from and describe how those items are prepared for eating.
periods.section_context: Plant-part food classification: roots (carrot, radish, beetroot), leaves (spinach, fenugreek, cabbage, mustard, coriander), fruits (guava, sapota, apple, mango), stems (potato, bamboo shoots, ginger, onion), seeds (grains, pulses, dry fruits).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Can you think of a vegetable your family cooks that is actually a fruit of the plant — like tomato or brinjal?' This sharpens the distinction between everyday language and botanical categories. Allow grouped tables of four so children can share picture cards easily.

periods.activity_title: Animal-Based Foods and the Water Puzzle
periods.textbook_anchor: Where does food come from? — Do you know which foods are grown in the fields? Write a few names of such crops (p. 105)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 105 list of animal-based foods

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'We sorted plant foods last time — now, what foods do we get from animals?' Children brainstorm freely. The teacher notes responses and then asks: 'Are there any foods you eat every day that come from neither a plant nor an animal?' This sets up the puzzle.

Children open Textbook p. 105 and read about animal-based foods — milk, curd, ghee, cheese, paneer, honey, eggs, meat. They discuss in pairs which of these their families eat and in what form, then write a short list in their notebooks: animal product on one side, cooked or processed form on the other (e.g. milk → kheer, paneer, curd).

The class tackles the puzzle: name foods that come from neither plants nor animals. Children suggest salt and water. The teacher guides discussion on why water is essential — especially during physical activity and in summer — linking hydration to the food chapter's nutrition strand.

Children discuss: 'Which crops are grown in fields near your home or in your village?' They write three to five field-crop names in their notebooks. The teacher closes with an open question: 'If you could only eat foods from one source — plants or animals — what would you miss most, and why?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify and describe animal-based food sources and explain the role of water and field crops in everyday diet.
periods.section_context: Animal-based foods (milk, curd, ghee, cheese, paneer, honey, eggs, meat), non-plant non-animal ingredients (salt, water), hydration during physical activity and summer, field crops.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does your family make any dairy product at home — like setting curd overnight or churning butter?' This surfaces traditional home food-making knowledge naturally. Ensure children who may not consume dairy or animal products feel included by framing questions around 'your family's foods' rather than universal assumptions.

periods.activity_title: Three Thalis — Drawing a Day of Meals
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Draw three plates or thalis with various food items, labelling food eaten in the morning, afternoon, and at night (p. 108)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 108 and reads the Draw prompt aloud. Children close their eyes and mentally 'walk through' their day: what they ate this morning, what they expect at lunch, what is typical at dinner in their home. A few children share aloud, revealing the variety across the class.

Each child draws three thalis or plates in their notebook — one for morning, one for afternoon, one for night — and labels every food item drawn. Children are encouraged to include foods from the chapter's categories: plant-based, animal-based, seasonal, and varied across food groups.

In groups of three, children display their thalis and notice: Which thali looks most varied? Is there a food that appeared in all three of their morning thalis? Do their dinner thalis look similar or very different? Groups share one striking observation with the class.

The teacher invites a brief whole-class reflection: 'Looking at all three thalis together, how balanced does your day of eating look?' Children respond orally — no written task required here — leaving the day's eating pattern as the takeaway thought.

periods.implied_lo: Students can present a day's worth of food choices through labelled drawings and evaluate variety across meals.
periods.section_context: Three thalis (morning, afternoon, night meals), labelled food items, variety across food groups, balanced day of eating.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Is there a food your family always eats at a particular meal — something that would feel wrong at a different time of day?' This surfaces meal-time food traditions naturally. Accept all drawings as valid — the goal is representation of what children actually eat, not an ideal diet.

periods.activity_title: Food We Eat — Bringing It All Together
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Why is it important to avoid wasting food? Can you think of some ways to reduce food waste at home? (p. 108)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 108 and poses the four Discuss questions one at a time — why we need different kinds of food, why we eat seasonal foods, how we can tell healthy from unhealthy food, and why food waste matters. Children respond in pairs first, then share with the class, drawing on everything the chapter has explored.

The class focuses on food waste: children discuss in small groups why wasting food is a concern — linking it to the effort of growing crops, the people who grow them, and the seasonal nature of produce. Each group lists two practical ways to reduce food waste at home and shares them with the class. The teacher records suggestions on the board.

Children tackle the guest-food scenario from Textbook p. 108: 'A guest arrives at your home — what food would you serve and why?' They write three to four sentences in their notebooks, thinking about variety, seasonal produce available, and hospitality. Children volunteer to share their answers, surfacing the cultural value of welcoming guests with food.

The teacher brings the chapter to a close with a final open question: 'From everything this chapter explored — your favourite dishes, Shirin's story, seasonal produce, plant and animal sources — what is the one thing about food you will think about differently now?' Children share a word or phrase each, making the synthesis personal and unhurried.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect food choices, food sources, and seasonal availability to values of reducing waste and practising hospitality, and articulate a personal food-awareness commitment.
periods.section_context: Food waste and ways to reduce it, healthy vs. unhealthy food, seasonal eating rationale, guest hospitality and food, variety across food groups, fruit chaat sharing activity.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone in your family ever talked about not wasting food — maybe quoting a saying or telling a story about a time when food was scarce?' This brings in intergenerational and regional food values naturally. Keep the final sharing round genuinely open — a single word is enough for a child who is reflective but quiet.

assessment_items.task: Think of two of your favourite homemade foods. For each one, draw a picture and write its name. Then write one word that describes its taste — sweet, sour, spicy, or bitter.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Food 1: [Draw here] Name: __________ Taste: __________
Food 2: [Draw here] Name: __________ Taste: __________
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any homemade dish the child names. The taste word need not be the only taste in the dish — the child's perception is valid. Regional and home-specific dishes are equally correct. Look for the link between the named dish and the taste word chosen.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent personal food knowledge through labelled drawings and connect dishes to taste categories.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The child can name and visually represent familiar food from personal experience and attach an appropriate taste category to each dish, showing that they have connected food to the four tastes introduced in this section.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold prompts one drawing and one taste word per dish. A child who names both dishes but leaves the taste word blank has represented food but not demonstrated taste-category connection — prompt them to choose one of the four words.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: accurately named dish with a recognisable drawing and a plausible taste word. Weak: a drawing with no name, or a taste word that cannot be linked to the dish described.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who find drawing difficult may write a description of the dish instead. Children who speak a language other than the medium of instruction may name the dish in their home language alongside the translation.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: labelled drawing with written taste word
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing is the primary mode introduced in this section's task; the taste word anchors the visual representation to the chapter's conceptual content about taste diversity.

assessment_items.question_text: Shirin was a good runner but she often fell sick. Her food at home then changed to include more variety — vegetables, fruits, different grains, pulses, and nuts. After this change, she stopped falling sick and ran better. Give two reasons why eating a variety of foods helped Shirin stay healthy and perform better.
expected_elements: Eating a variety of foods provides different things the body needs (e.g., strength, energy, protection from sickness).
Relying on only a few food items means the body misses out on what other foods provide.
Home-cooked varied meals supported Shirin's recovery and athletic performance.
assessment_items.annotation: Award credit for any two distinct reasons that connect food variety to health or performance. The child need not use technical nutritional terms. Accept reasoning such as 'different foods make different parts of the body strong' as a valid response.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain why variety across food groups supports physical well-being, using evidence from a narrative.

assessment_items.question_text: In summer, people in many parts of India prefer to eat juicy fruits and drink cool drinks. In winter, they prefer warm soups and stews. What is the main reason for this difference?

options.label: A
options.text: Cool drinks and warm soups cost the same amount, so people choose based on habit.

options.label: B
options.text: Different fruits and vegetables grow in different seasons, so the foods available change with the weather.

options.label: C
options.text: People in India only know how to cook certain foods and do not change their recipes.

options.label: D
options.text: The government tells people which foods to eat in each season.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is A. Seasonal availability of produce is the key concept from this section. Responses B, C, and D represent common reasoning errors rather than chapter-based misconceptions and serve to confirm that the child is reasoning about natural availability rather than guessing.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can record and organise observations about how seasonal availability shapes food choices in their local and wider environment.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

what_each_option_reveals.C: The child has not connected the section's content to the idea of seasonal produce and instead attributes food differences to limited cooking knowledge — missing the natural-environment link entirely.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child is reasoning by a non-relevant factor (cost) rather than engaging with the chapter's explanation of seasonal availability.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child attributes food choices to external authority rather than to the natural cycle of seasonal produce — a misplacement of agency.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at these four food items: carrot, mango, potato, spinach. For each one, write which part of the plant it comes from.
assessment_items.annotation: All four correct answers are required for full credit; partial credit may be awarded for two or three correct. Potato as a stem is the most commonly misclassified item — accept 'underground stem' as correct. Do not penalise spelling as long as the plant-part category is clear.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify everyday food items by the plant part they come from and describe how those items are prepared for eating.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

expected_elements: Potato — stem (underground stem is also acceptable)

assessment_items.question_text: Paneer is made from milk. Which of the following correctly describes the source of milk and the food group paneer belongs to?

options.label: A
options.text: Milk comes from animals; paneer is a plant-based food because it is white like milk from a cow that eats grass.

options.label: B
options.text: Milk comes from animals; paneer is an animal-based food.

options.label: C
options.text: Milk comes from plants; paneer is a plant-based food.

options.label: D
options.text: Paneer comes from neither plants nor animals, like salt and water.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is A. Options B, C, and D each represent a specific confusion introduced during the animal-source and puzzle discussion. Option D is particularly diagnostic — it shows the child has overgeneralised the salt-and-water puzzle to dairy products.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify and describe animal-based food sources and explain the role of water and field crops in everyday diet.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.C: The child has not registered the animal-source category for dairy products and incorrectly assigns milk to plants — a foundational classification error from this section.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child correctly identifies the animal source of milk but then applies confused causal reasoning (the cow eats grass, therefore the product is plant-based) — mixing the food chain with food categorisation.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child has overgeneralised the salt-and-water puzzle from this unit to all white or processed foods, failing to distinguish the special non-plant-non-animal category from dairy products.

assessment_items.task: Draw three plates or thalis in your notebook — one for morning, one for afternoon, and one for night. In each plate, draw and label at least two food items you eat at that meal. After you finish, look at all three plates together and answer: Does your day include foods from more than one food group? Write one sentence about what you notice.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Morning thali: [Draw here] Food items: __________ __________
Afternoon thali: [Draw here] Food items: __________ __________
Night thali: [Draw here] Food items: __________ __________
What I notice about my day of eating: __________
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any culturally valid food items for each meal — there is no single correct set of foods. The reflection sentence should show some awareness of variety or sameness across the three thalis; it need not use technical terms. Regional and family-specific meal patterns are equally correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can present a day's worth of food choices through labelled drawings and evaluate variety across meals.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The child can represent a complete day of eating visually and in writing, and can evaluate their own food choices for variety — connecting the drawing task to the chapter's concept of a balanced, varied diet.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Each thali requires at least two labelled items. If a child draws items but does not label them, prompt labelling before accepting the product. The reflection sentence is the key evaluation step — a child who draws three identical thalis and writes 'I eat the same food every day' has demonstrated genuine self-observation.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: three distinct thalis with labelled foods from different food groups, and a reflection sentence that identifies whether variety is present. Weak: identical items across all three thalis with no reflection, or drawings with no labels.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who find drawing difficult may write food names in the thali outline instead of drawing. Children may represent their actual daily food even if it is simple or repetitive — the task values honest self-representation over an ideal diet.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing three thalis is the textbook's own task for this section; adding a written reflection sentence elevates the activity from representation to evaluation, matching the implied_lo's 'evaluate variety' demand.

assessment_items.question_text: Why is it important not to waste food? Give two reasons and describe one thing you could do at home to reduce food waste.
look_for: At least two distinct reasons for not wasting food — for example: growing food requires effort from farmers; wasting food means others who need it go without; wasted food can harm the environment.
A concrete, actionable suggestion for reducing waste at home — for example: taking only as much as you can eat, using leftovers the next day, storing food properly.
A response that connects the food in the chapter (seasonal produce, home-cooked meals) to the idea that food has value and effort behind it.
Clear reasoning rather than a simple list — the child should explain why the reason matters, not just name it.
assessment_items.annotation: Award credit for genuine reasoning. A child who writes 'because food is important' without elaboration has not demonstrated the ECR-level response; look for at least one expanded reason. The home-waste-reduction suggestion may be simple and practical — there is no single correct answer.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect food choices, food sources, and seasonal availability to values of reducing waste and practising hospitality, and articulate a personal food-awareness commitment.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)
